extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and political thinkers (late-18th-century British public) interested in assessing governments and the French Revolution
extracted.subtask_description: A normative framework for judging the effects, legitimacy, and health of a government (especially debates between monarchy and democracy), using demographic, economic, institutional, and moral evidence. Focuses on whether abuses demand abolition or reform and on the practical causes of public disorder rather than abstract labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the population
rubrics_metrics.description: Population flourishing and progressive improvement is a key standard for estimating the effects of government on a country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use population size, growth, and trends (e.g., contemporaneous reports: Intendants' estimates, M. Necker, Dr. Price) as evidence; consider emigration, urban unemployment, and decline (e.g., Paris population decline, reported unemployment and mendicancy) as signs of governmental failure or national distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth of the country (quantity, distribution, circulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wealth of a country is another important standard: total riches, equality of distribution, and readiness of circulation indicate how protective or destructive a government is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine coinage/specie, bullion and mint records (Necker's coinage/specie figures cited), public accounts, and indicators of domestic circulation; reasonable deductions from reliable financial accounts can indicate whether industry and property are discouraged or encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material infrastructure and public works
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence and quality of roads, bridges, canals, ports, harbors, fortifications, and naval apparatus are measures of a state's health and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey observable public works (high roads, bridges, canals, ports, fortifications) and level of municipal and national investment as evidence that the government has fostered commerce, defense, and public utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures, arts, and learned culture
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of manufactures, the arts that polish life, and the production of learned men (statesmen, lawyers, philosophers, poets, etc.) are signs of a flourishing society under its government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the quality and reputation of manufactures and cultural life (e.g., literature, science, theology, criticism) as part of national prosperity and the corrective to claims of universal despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public economy and administration (incl. fiscal records)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system of public economy and the aggregate charges and accounts indicate the state's condition and whether abuses are systemic or remediable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate official financial records and extraordinary charges (e.g., mysterious large charges, grain account discrepancies) and whether assemblies inquire into them; extraordinary unexplained expenditures may point to secret expenses or revolutionary mismanagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for reform versus need for total revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether existing abuses could have been corrected by reformation rather than requiring the total destruction of the social fabric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at contemporary demands (e.g., instructions to representatives calling for reformation not destruction), recent reform efforts, openness of the government to projects of improvement, and whether abuses are removable by constitutional changes rather than violent overthrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of majority tyranny under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy may resemble a tyranny because a majority can exercise severe oppression upon minorities; the degree of division affects this danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether strong divisions exist that enable popular persecution, and whether victims of such persecution are deprived of external consolation; judge the vulnerability of minorities and the potential for collective cruelty under popular rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative adaptability of forms (monarchy's flexibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchy may be preferable in some respects because republican elements can be more readily grafted onto a monarchy than monarchical elements onto a republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh historical evidence and practical capacity for blending institutions: a system that allows gradual incorporation of representative elements may be more stable than an experiment in pure democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and conduct of the nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The behavior of the nobility—treatment of inferior classes, land tenure practices, military monopoly, hospitality, and local civil power—matters to whether they deserve punishment or reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess concrete conduct (e.g., cruelty, oppression, land-letting practices, military exclusivity) rather than abstract privileges; distinguish between genuine abuses and exaggerations used to justify confiscation or abolition; note that many nobles may exhibit humane conduct and public-spiritedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and culpability of the clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge clergy on the basis of observable individual vices and abuses, not by wholesale collective punishment founded on historical instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate past institutional crimes from present individuals' conduct; beware of 'raking into the histories of former ages' to justify plunder; ensure punishments are proportionate and targeted rather than collective confiscation based on corporate succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of history and avoidance of collective guilt
rubrics_metrics.description: History should be used to instruct about causes, not perverted to supply pretexts for vengeance; do not punish people for the crimes of their ancestors or of a corporate body as if eternal guilt attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply remedies to underlying causes and permanent vices, not merely to names or antiquated pretexts; avoid historical perversion that supplies parties with weapons for contemporary factionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and remedy underlying vices causing public disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of civil storms are moral vices (pride, ambition, avarice, revenge, lust, sedition, hypocrisy, ungoverned zeal), not merely forms of government or legal institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct reforms and remedies at these permanent human vices and their institutional manifestations rather than at superficial changes of titles or removal of particular offices; recognize that the same vices assume new forms across ages and require practical remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of rhetorical/populist leaders and performative remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders of clubs and coffee-houses who 'speak with sovereign contempt' and use show, tumult, and alarms to distract from indigence are indicative of poor governance and dangerous politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quality of leadership and political rhetoric: be skeptical of quackish parade and performative displays that aim to drown out real cries of indigence; check whether legislative actions (e.g., committees, taxes for poor relief) are substantive or mere theater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality and justice in punishment and reform
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to degrade or punish whole orders (nobility, clergy) wholesale; punishments should be proportionate and targeted to actual culpability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider instructions, voluntary surrender of privileges (e.g., contributions), and whether abuses were widespread enough to merit confiscation; reforms that merely degrade status without remedying causes are condemned.
